questions: Why do the sample means cluster around the true mean rather than spreading evenly everywhere?
If n grows from 25 to 100, by what factor does the spread of the sample mean shrink?
segments.say: The sampling distribution of the mean shrinks as n grows. Take the mean of a sample and repeat many times: the sample means cluster around the true mean. Watch the five dots scatter widely when n = 2, then pull in tight when n = 25 - the spread of the means shrinks by root n, so the n = 25 curve stands taller and narrower. Make the root-n shrink your reflex for every sampling question in this topic.

questions: What exactly does the shaded tail area beyond the observed statistic represent?
A test returns p = 0.31 at the 5% level - what is the verdict, and why?
segments.say: Hypothesis testing: the p-value decides against α. State the null and the alternative first, then ask how surprising the data would be if the null were true. Watch the tail beyond the observed statistic: its area is the p-value. At p = 0.31 the null stands, but as the statistic slides out and p drops below alpha = 0.05, the verdict flips to reject. Check your student notes for the p-against-alpha picture before we meet the trap.

questions: In one sentence, what is the 3% in a p-value of 0.03 actually counting?
Why can a p-value, computed assuming the null is true, never be the probability that the null is true?
segments.say: The p-value trap: it is not P(H₀ is true). A p-value of 0.03 does not mean the null has a 3% chance of being true. Repeat the test 100 times while the null is true: about 3 of those repeats give data this extreme, and that count of repeats is all the 3% ever meant. Now open the worksheet and try the p-value question in pairs, watching your own wording as you explain it.
segments.watchFor: A p-value of 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true. Listen and look for it on the worksheet and in pair talk: any answer turning 0.03 into a probability about the null itself shows the trap reading, not the data-given-the-null reading - send them back to the 100 repeats under the null.

questions: Which cell of the table is the false alarm, and which quantity caps how often it happens?
In the exit ticket, which question tests the p-value trap - and what answer shows you have it?
segments.say: Type I and Type II errors: the two ways to be wrong. Lay out the table: reality across the top, our decision down the side. Rejecting a true null is the Type I false alarm, capped by alpha; accepting a false null is the Type II missed signal, fought with power = 1 - beta and bigger samples. Compare the error table in your student notes one last time. Now the exit ticket - on your own, no talking - covering the sampling distribution, the p-against-alpha verdict, the p-value trap and the two error types.
